newsitem.title: FINLAND: HUHTAMAKI, CULTOR DOWNPLAY XYLITOL TAX RELIEF.
newsitem.headline: HUHTAMAKI, CULTOR DOWNPLAY XYLITOL TAX RELIEF.

text.p: Finnish Cultor and Huhtamaki said on Thursday the tax exemption on xylitol which the EU Commission is demanding Finland to abolish was not materially significant for the companies.

For confectionery and packaging group Huhtamaki -- which uses birch sweetener xylitol in some products including Finland's biggest candy product Xylitol Jenkki chewing gum -- scrapping the tax relief would be no big deal.
"It would have no material impact," Huhtamaki head of communications Markku Pietinen told Reuters. "The price increasing effect of the tax would not be very large."

But for food, sweetener and bakery group Cultor, which producers the sweetener, the EU's demands are important in principle since the commission has rejected research showing that xylitor reduces dental caries and plaque when eaten regularly.

"From our point of view, this is a big issue in principle ... it seems incomprensible that the EU does not use research showing (the effects) but leans on older reports," said Cultor corporate communications vice president Raija Kariola.

Kariola said the sweets tax -- used in Denmark and Finland where it is 3.50 markka per kilogramme -- would be very small for the sweets where xylitol is typically used and doubted that it would change Finnish consumer behaviour.
She estimated that the tax would be only "a couple of penni" per package of chewing gum, retailing at about 2.50 markka.

The European Commission said on March 11 in a written response to a Finnish MEP's question that the studies Finland claim show the effects of xylitol used "insufficent methodology" and could not prove xylitol had different effects than similar substances, like sorbitol, which are not freed from the tax.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has made a similar conclusion, the commission said.
It said it would start a process against Finland to end the discriminating taxation.

The Finnish industry's target is that Finland would abolish the sweetener tax altogether, which would also remove the problem with xylitol. State revenue from the sweets tax is about 150 million markka per year, a finance ministry official said.
Total tax revenue in this year's 191 billion markka budget is 132 billion markka.
